title: Aeneae naves. Ardea
titleEn: The Ships of Aeneas; the Fall of Ardea — Metamorphoses XIV.527–580
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The Rutulian envoys come back with the news that Aetolian help is refused, the war goes on, and Turnus carries fire to the Trojan fleet. Cybele, whose sacred pines on Ida were felled to build those ships, fills the air with the noise of her own rites and tells Turnus his fire will come to nothing; thunder answers, the winds go to war, and the burning hulls are turned into sea-nymphs part by part — stern into head, oars into fingers, keel into spine. The fighting does not stop for the portent: both sides have gods, and shame at giving up keeps them at it until Turnus falls and Ardea falls with him. Out of the warm ash a bird rises that keeps the taken city’s cry, its gauntness, its pallor and its name.

sentences.t:
Hinc ubi legati rediere, negata ferentes
arma Aetola sibi,
sentences.l: From here, when the envoys returned, bringing back the Aetolian arms denied to them,
sentences.i: When the envoys came back from there with the answer that Aetolian arms were refused them,
sentences.n: rediere is rediērunt, the poetic third-plural perfect, and it recurs constantly: odere, videre and supposuere all turn up later in this part. negata … arma Aetola sibi is the object of ferentes, so what the envoys carry home is not weapons but the refusal of them — Latin compresses “they brought word that the Aetolian arms were denied” into the arms themselves being carried back. sibi, dative, points back to the Rutulians who sent the embassy, and Aetola names the help sought from Diomedes, whose line came from Calydon in Aetolia.

sentences.l: the Rutulians without those forces wage the wars they had set in array, and much of blood is given from either side;
sentences.i: the Rutulians fight the war they had already marshalled, and without that help, and much blood is paid on both sides;
sentences.n: instructa is a military word, “drawn up in line”, so bella instructa gerunt means they fight the war they had already prepared, now short of the strength they had counted on. cruoris is a partitive genitive after multum, “much of blood”; cruor is blood spilt and seen, not the blood in the veins, which is sanguis. datur is passive with nobody named as giving, which lets the cost fall on both sides at once.

sentences.t:
fert ecce avidas in pinea Turnus
texta faces, ignesque timent, quibus unda pepercit.
sentences.l: look, Turnus brings greedy torches against the pine-woven work, and they fear fires, they to whom the wave had been sparing.
sentences.i: and see: Turnus carries ravening torches against the pine-built hulls, and the ships that the sea had spared now go in fear of fire.
sentences.n: pinea texta, “woven pine”, is the ships: verse regularly names a ship by the timber it is built from, and the word for weaving suits a hull of fitted planks. avidas, “greedy”, is transferred from the flame to the torches that carry it. parco governs the dative, so quibus is “to whom the wave had been sparing”, which is why the literal keeps that odd English instead of a plain “whom the sea spared”; pepercit is perfect, and against the present timent English wants a pluperfect. Its antecedent is the ships, supplied from the subject of timent. ecce drops the narrator into the scene: the reader is told to look.

sentences.t:
Iamque picem et ceras alimentaque cetera flammae
Mulciber urebat perque altum ad carbasa malum
ibat, et incurvae fumabant transtra carinae:
sentences.l: And already Mulciber was burning the pitch and the waxes and the other feedings of the flame, and was going up along the tall mast to the sailcloth, and the cross-benches of the curved keel were smoking:
sentences.i: And by now the fire was eating the pitch and the wax and everything else that feeds a flame, and running up the tall mast to the canvas, and the thwarts of the curved hull were smoking:
sentences.n: Mulciber is a cult title of Vulcan standing here by metonymy for the fire itself — the god’s name doing the work of the common noun, which is why the verb is the ordinary urebat. The three imperfects urebat, ibat and fumabant hold the scene open and unfinished, which is exactly what the cum of the next unit needs. carbasa is a Greek loan-word for the fine linen of a sail; transtra are the rowers’ cross-benches, laid athwart the hull.

sentences.t:
cum memor has pinus Idaeo vertice caesas
sancta deum genetrix tinnitibus aera pulsi
aeris et inflati complevit murmure buxi,
sentences.l: when, mindful that these pines had been cut on the Idaean summit, the holy mother of the gods filled the air with the ringings of struck bronze and with the drone of blown boxwood,
sentences.i: when the holy mother of the gods, remembering that these pines had been felled on Ida’s peak, filled the sky with the clash of beaten bronze and the moan of the blown boxwood pipe,
sentences.n: This is the inverted cum: after a run of imperfects the turn of the narrative arrives inside the cum clause, so English wants “when suddenly”. memor takes has pinus … caesas as an accusative with participle, with esse understood — “mindful that these pines had been cut”. deum is the old genitive plural for deorum, “of the gods”. aera is the Greek accusative singular of aer, “the air”, and it is what she fills; do not confuse it with aeris in the very next line, which belongs to aes, “bronze”. The struck bronze and the blown boxwood pipe are the noise of Cybele’s own worship, and the grove on Ida that gave the timber for the fleet is hers, which is the whole ground of her claim.

sentences.t:
perque leves domitis invecta leonibus auras
“inrita sacrilega iactas incendia dextra,
Turne!” ait.
sentences.l: and, carried through the light airs by tamed lions: “Ineffectual fires you hurl with sacrilegious right hand, Turnus!” she says.
sentences.i: and, borne through the light air by her tamed lions, she says: “The fires you fling with that sacrilegious hand come to nothing, Turnus!”
sentences.n: invecta is a perfect participle agreeing with the goddess, “having been carried”, and Latin hangs the whole journey on it where English would rather have a clause. The lion-drawn car is Cybele’s standard equipment. inrita is proleptic: the fires are not fruitless yet, they are called fruitless by the outcome she is about to impose on them. dextra is ablative, the hand as instrument, and sacrilega names the act as robbery from a shrine — which is what burning her own pines amounts to. ait is a present in the middle of past narrative.

sentences.t:
“Eripiam, nec me patiente cremabit
ignis edax nemorum partes et membra meorum.”
sentences.l: “I shall snatch them away, and not with me allowing it shall the devouring fire burn up the parts and the limbs of my groves.”
sentences.i: “I shall carry them off; not while I permit it shall the greedy fire burn the pieces and the limbs of my own woods.”
sentences.n: me patiente is an ablative absolute built on a present participle, literally “with me allowing it”, which English turns into a clause, “while I allow it”. nec negates the whole clause and not merely the absolute. membra, “limbs”, treats the felled pines as parts of a body: the ships are dismembered pieces of her grove, which is why she can call them meorum and take them back.

sentences.t:
Intonuit dicente dea, tonitrumque secuti
cum saliente graves ceciderunt grandine nimbi,
sentences.l: It thundered while the goddess was speaking, and, having followed the thunder, heavy storm-clouds came down with leaping hail,
sentences.i: It thundered as the goddess spoke, and after the thunder heavy squalls came down with hail that bounced where it struck,
sentences.n: dicente dea is an ablative absolute of the simultaneous kind, “with the goddess speaking”, that is, before she had finished. Intonuit has no expressed subject: weather verbs stand impersonally in Latin, “it thundered”, and the thunder answers her while she is still speaking, without anyone having to say whose it is. secuti is a perfect participle agreeing with nimbi, “having followed”. saliente is the participle used of hail bouncing as it lands.

sentences.t:
aeraque et tumidum subitis concursibus aequor
Astraei turbant et eunt in proelia fratres.
sentences.l: and the air and the swollen sea, with sudden clashings, the Astraean brothers throw into confusion, and they go into battles.
sentences.i: and the sons of Astraeus churn the air and the heaving sea with sudden collisions, and go to war with one another.
sentences.n: Astraei … fratres, “the Astraean brothers”, are the winds: Astraei is the adjective, not a genitive, and the brothers are Astraeus’ sons, not his brothers. Astraei opens line 545 and fratres closes it, with both verbs standing between the adjective and its noun, so the reader does not learn who the subject is until the sentence ends. aera is again the Greek accusative singular of aer, “the air”, paired with aequor, “the sea’s level”, so the storm takes both elements at once. eunt in proelia makes the winds combatants: the storm is a battle they fight against each other.

sentences.l: And out of these the fostering mother, having used the strength of one, broke off the hempen hawsers of the Phrygian ship and carries the vessels headlong and sinks them beneath mid-sea;
sentences.i: And using the strength of one of them, the nursing mother snapped the hempen mooring-ropes of the Phrygian fleet, drove the hulls down head-first and plunged them under the open sea;
sentences.n: E quibus is a connecting relative — “and out of these” — carrying the winds over from the sentence before; Latin opens a new sentence with a relative where English starts a fresh one. usa is the perfect participle of the deponent utor, active in meaning, and utor governs the ablative: viribus is what she used. Watch the tenses inside the one sentence: praerupit is perfect, then fert and mergit are present, and the historic present takes over just as the ships go down. Magnus prints puppis, “of the ship”; The Latin Library prints classis, “of the fleet” — a singular standing for the whole fleet either way.

sentences.t:
robore mollito lignoque in corpora verso
in capitum facies puppes mutantur aduncae,
sentences.l: with the oak softened and the timber turned into bodies, the hooked sterns are changed into the likeness of heads,
sentences.i: the oak grew soft, the timber turned into flesh, and the curving sterns changed into the shape of heads,
sentences.n: Two ablative absolutes are stacked here, robore mollito and ligno … verso, and they carry the change itself while the main clause reports only one of its results; English prefers finite verbs, “the oak softened and the wood turned”. mutantur is passive here with no agent named at all — the transformation simply happens, and nobody is said to work it. puppes aduncae are the sterns of ancient ships, which rose in a hook above the water: that curve is what makes them heads.

sentences.t: in digitos abeunt et crura natantia remi,
sentences.l: the oars pass away into fingers and swimming legs,
sentences.i: the oars turn into fingers and into legs that swim,
sentences.n: abeunt in, “go away into”, governs two accusatives at once, digitos and crura, and it stands among the other verbs of change working through this catalogue — verso, mutantur, mutatur and fiunt. natantia is a present participle doing an adjective’s work: the legs are made for swimming from the moment they exist. The oars become both fingers and legs because both are what drives a body through water.

sentences.t:
quodque prius fuerat, latus est mediisque carina
subdita navigiis spinae mutatur in usum,
sentences.l: and what it had been before, it is — a side; and the keel set beneath the middle of the vessels is changed into the use of a spine,
sentences.i: the flank stays what it was, a flank; and the keel that ran under the middle of the hulls becomes a backbone,
sentences.n: quodque prius fuerat, latus est is one of the two items in the catalogue that do not change — the other is the colour at 555: a ship’s side is already a flank, so the transformation leaves it where it is. mediis … navigiis is dative after subdita, since subdo takes the dative of the thing set under. spinae in usum is “into the use of a spine”, that is, into a spine’s function — Latin names the job the part will do rather than the part itself.

sentences.t:
lina comae molles, antemnae bracchia fiunt,
caerulus, ut fuerat, color est;
sentences.l: the sailcloths become soft hair, the yard-arms arms; the colour is sea-blue, as it had been;
sentences.i: the sails become soft hair, the yards become arms; the colour is sea-dark, just as it was;
sentences.n: One verb, fiunt, serves both clauses: lina and antemnae are the subjects, comae molles and bracchia the predicate nouns, and Latin does not repeat the verb for the second pair. lina, “linens”, is the sailcloth; antemnae are the yard-arms crossing the mast, and a horizontal spar reaching out on either side is the obvious thing to turn into arms. caerulus is the dark blue-green of the sea, and ut fuerat marks the colour as the second thing that has nothing to change into, after the side at 552.

sentences.t:
quasque ante timebant,
illas virgineis exercent lusibus undas
naides aequoreae durisque in montibus ortae
molle fretum celebrant nec eas sua tangit origo.
sentences.l: and the waves which they feared before, those the sea-naiads work with maidenly sports, and, sprung on hard mountains, they throng the soft sea, nor does their own origin touch them.
sentences.i: and the waters they once feared they now ply in maiden games; sea-nymphs, born on harsh mountains, they crowd the yielding sea, and their origin does not trouble them.
sentences.n: quas … illas … undas puts the relative clause in front of its own antecedent, which is normal in Latin and has to be reversed in English: “those waves which they feared”. timebant is imperfect, their old and repeated fear, held against the present exercent and celebrant. The contrast is carried by two pairs of adjectives, duris montibus against molle fretum, hard against soft, and the last clause turns it: nec eas sua tangit origo, their own origin does not touch them, so the mountain-born timber feels no pull back to the hills. tangit is “touch” in the sense of affect or move.

sentences.t:
Non tamen oblitae, quam multa pericula saepe
pertulerint pelago, iactatis saepe carinis
supposuere manus, nisi siqua vehebat Achivos:
sentences.l: Yet not having forgotten how many perils they had often endured on the deep, they have often put their hands beneath tossed keels, unless any ship was carrying Achaeans:
sentences.i: They have not forgotten, though, how many dangers they often bore at sea, and they have often set a hand under a storm-tossed hull — unless it was carrying Greeks:
sentences.n: oblitae is the perfect participle of the deponent obliviscor, active in meaning, “having forgotten”, and non negates it. quam multa pericula … pertulerint is an indirect question, which is why its verb is subjunctive. iactatis … carinis is dative after supposuere, because you put a hand under something; supposuere is the poetic third-plural perfect again. nisi siqua is nisi si qua, “unless if any”, with the noun for ship left to be supplied — the indefinite qua is the form the pronoun takes after si.

sentences.t:
cladis adhuc Phrygiae memores, odere Pelasgos
Neritiaeque ratis viderunt fragmina laetis
vultibus et laetis videre rigescere puppem
vultibus Alcinoi saxumque increscere ligno.
sentences.l: still mindful of the Phrygian disaster, they hate the Pelasgians, and with glad faces they saw the fragments of the Neritian ship, and with glad faces they saw the stern of Alcinous stiffen and stone grow over the wood.
sentences.i: the ruin of Troy is still with them, and they hate the Greeks: with glad faces they saw the wreckage of Ithaca’s ship, with glad faces they saw the Phaeacian vessel harden and stone spread over its timber.
sentences.n: odere is the perfect of odi, a verb that exists only in perfect forms and carries a present sense, “they hate”. memores takes the genitive cladis Phrygiae, “mindful of the Phrygian disaster”, that is, of the fall of Troy — the nymphs remember it because they were Trojan ships. Pelasgos is one of the old poetic names for the Greeks, like Achivos in the line before. Ovid uses viderunt in line 563 and videre in line 564 for the same tense, the second being the poetic third-plural perfect, and the variation is metrical convenience. laetis vultibus is split across the line-end twice over, and both times the noun is held back to open the next line: laetis closes 563 and vultibus opens 564; then the second laetis stands inside 564, not at its end, and its vultibus opens 565. The Neritian ship is Ulysses’, named from Neritos on Ithaca; Alcinous is king of the Phaeacians, and Neptune turned the ship that ferried Ulysses home to stone, which is the stiffening described here.

sentences.t:
Spes erat, in nymphas animata classe marinas,
posse metu monstri Rutulum desistere bello:
sentences.l: There was hope, with the fleet quickened into sea-nymphs, that the Rutulian could leave off from war through fear of the portent:
sentences.i: There was hope that, now the fleet had come alive as sea-nymphs, fear of the marvel would make the Rutulian give up the war:
sentences.n: in nymphas animata classe marinas is an ablative absolute with the noun phrase pulled apart around it: in nymphas stands early in the line and marinas closes it, with animata classe held between them. spes erat then governs an accusative and infinitive, Rutulum … posse desistere, “hope that the Rutulian could leave off”. desisto takes the ablative bello, and metu is an ablative of cause. monstrum is a portent, a thing shown as a sign from the gods, not a monster. Rutulum is accusative singular, the Rutulian, meaning Turnus himself.

sentences.t:
perstat, habetque deos pars utraque, quodque deorum est
instar, habent animos;
sentences.l: he stands firm, and each side has gods, and — what is the match of gods — they have spirit;
sentences.i: he holds out; both sides have gods behind them, and what stands in for gods, they have courage;
sentences.n: perstat is singular and its subject is the Rutulian of the line before. The sentence then swings to pars utraque, “each side”, with a singular verb habet, and then to a plural habent for the men on both sides, so the grammar itself widens from one man to two armies. instar is an indeclinable neuter noun meaning the equivalent or match of a thing, and it governs the genitive deorum. The point of the line is that courage does the work gods are supposed to do.

sentences.t:
nec iam dotalia regna
nec sceptrum soceri, nec te, Lavinia virgo,
sentences.l: and now neither the dowry kingdoms nor the sceptre of the father-in-law, nor you, maiden Lavinia,
sentences.i: and now it is not the kingdom that comes with the bride, nor her father’s sceptre, nor you, maiden Lavinia,
sentences.n: The three objects hang unfinished until petunt arrives in the next unit, “they seek” — a long suspension that lets the list run before the reader learns it is a list of what they are no longer after. dotalia regna are the realms that come as the bride’s dowry, the war’s original prize. soceri, “of the father-in-law”, is Latinus, whose daughter both Aeneas and Turnus claim. nec te, Lavinia virgo is an apostrophe: the poem turns aside from its narrative to address the girl directly, and the vocative gives her a moment as a person before dropping her.

sentences.t:
sed vicisse petunt deponendique pudore
bella gerunt,
sentences.l: but they seek to have conquered, and out of shame at laying it down they wage wars,
sentences.i: what they want is to have won; shame at giving up keeps them fighting,
sentences.n: vicisse is a perfect infinitive where English expects a present: what they want is not the winning but the having won, the finished victory. deponendi is a gerund in the genitive after pudore, “shame of laying down” — of laying down the war, with bella supplied from the words that follow. pudore is an ablative of cause, so shame, not policy, is what keeps the fighting going, which is the sourest line in the passage.

sentences.t:
tandemque Venus victricia nati
arma videt,
sentences.l: and at last Venus sees the victorious arms of her son,
sentences.n: victricia is the neuter plural of victrix, the feminine agent-noun for a conqueror, used here as an adjective with arma — Latin makes a word for a victorious woman agree with weapons. nati, “of her son”, stands for Aeneas, named by what he is to her rather than by his own name. tandem, “at last”, measures the whole war from her side of it.

sentences.t:
Turnusque cadit, cadit Ardea, Turno
sospite dicta potens.
sentences.l: and Turnus falls, Ardea falls — called mighty with Turnus preserved.
sentences.i: and Turnus falls; Ardea falls, the city that was called mighty as long as Turnus lived.
sentences.n: cadit is repeated for the two falls, the man and then his city, and the present tense puts both in front of the reader as they happen. Turno sospite is an ablative absolute of time, “with Turnus safe and sound”, meaning while he was alive; sospes is a solemn old word, used of a person brought through danger unharmed. dicta potens is a perfect participle agreeing with Ardea, “called mighty”. Ardea was the Rutulian capital and Turnus’ own city, which is why one fall follows the other.

sentences.t:
Quem postquam barbarus ensis
abstulit et tepida latuerunt tecta favilla,
sentences.l: And after the barbarian sword had carried him off, and the roofs lay hidden under warm embers,
sentences.i: And when the barbarian sword had taken him, and the houses lay buried in warm ash,
sentences.n: Quem is a connecting relative opening a new sentence — “and after the sword had carried him off” — and the him is Turnus, killed at the end of the unit before. The two witnesses part company twice in this one line: Magnus prints Quem … ensis, “after the barbarian sword carried him off”; The Latin Library prints quam … ignis, “after the barbarian fire carried her off”, which makes the city rather than the man the thing destroyed. Both readings arrive at the same ashes. barbarus, “foreign”, is the Trojan side seen from the Italian one: to a Rutulian it is the incomers who are the barbarians. latuerunt … tecta is an intransitive lateo, “the roofs lay hidden”, with the ablative favilla for what hid them.

sentences.t:
congerie e media tum primum cognita praepes
subvolat et cineres plausis everberat alis.
sentences.l: from the middle of the heap, then for the first time known, a swift-flying bird flies up and lashes the ashes with clapped wings.
sentences.i: out of the middle of the heap a bird never seen before flies up and thrashes the ashes with clapping wings.
sentences.n: praepes is properly an adjective, “swift of flight”, used here as a noun for the bird, and cognita is feminine to agree with it. tum primum cognita, “then first known”, marks the moment a species begins: the bird did not exist before this and is recognised at the instant it appears. everberat is verbero with ex-, “beat thoroughly”, and plausis alis is an ablative of means built on a perfect participle — the wings have been clapped together, and the ash goes up.

sentences.l: Both the sound and the leanness and the pallor and everything that would befit a captured city, and the name of the city too, remained in her;
sentences.i: The cry, the gauntness, the pallor, everything that suits a city taken — and the city’s name as well — all of it stayed in her;
sentences.n: quae deceant is a relative clause of characteristic, and that is why its verb is subjunctive: “everything of a kind to suit a captured city”. mansit is singular although the subjects are strung together with et … et … et, because Latin lets the verb agree with the nearest of them, nomen. Here quoque is the adverb “also”, not quo-que, “and with which” — the same letters do both jobs and the choice has to be made every time. The name is the point of the whole aetiology: the heron is called ardea in Latin, so the city’s name goes on living in the bird’s.

sentences.t: et ipsa suis deplangitur Ardea pennis.
sentences.l: and Ardea herself is mourned with her own wings.
sentences.i: and Ardea is her own mourner, beating herself with her own wings.
sentences.n: deplangitur is the passive of deplango, which means to lament by beating the breast, so the one verb holds both the noise and the blows: the wings do to the bird exactly what a mourner’s hands do to a mourner. suis … pennis is an ablative of means, not an agent, since the wings are the instrument and not a person. ipsa makes the city its own mourner, and that is the last turn of the transformation — Ardea grieves for Ardea.
